title: The Divine Kabbalist Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri
content:
The Divine Kabbalist Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri

This overview presents the figure of Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri as a unique and connecting link between the ancient mystical tradition of Babylonian Jewry and modern Israeli reality. The text traces his spiritual development from his roots in Baghdad and under the influence of the "Ben Ish Ḥai," through his immigration to Jerusalem, where he combined extreme modesty and manual labor with unprecedented depth in esoteric Torah. The author of the article emphasizes that the Rabbi's power derived not only from performing "miracles," but from an ordered system that sanctifies restraint of speech and silence as tools for attaining spiritual power and hastening the redemption. Alongside analysis of his public work and the establishment of the "Naḥalat Yitzḥak" institution, the source surveys the Rabbi's written legacy and practical Kabbalah, thereby seeking to assess his decisive influence on religious, social and political identity in the State of Israel.

The Divine Kabbalist Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri: A Historiographic, Theological and Sociological Examination of His Work and Teachings

The figure of Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri (1899–2006) constitutes one of the most fascinating religious and social phenomena of the last hundred years in the history of the Jewish people. As one who earned the epithet "the elder of the kabbalists," Rabbi Kaduri stood at a unique crossroads between the ancient mystical tradition of Babylonian Jewry and modern Israeli reality, saturated with political and social tensions. His work is not limited merely to the narrow domain of writing amulets or giving blessings, but rather reflects a broad system of Torah teachings, spiritual leadership and preservation of kabbalistic traditions that were in danger of extinction with the destruction of the Torah centers in the Eastern lands. Understanding his figure requires in-depth analysis of his roots in Baghdad, his development in the yeshivot of Jerusalem, and his unique worldview regarding redemption, the sanctity of speech and practical Kabbalah.[1, 2, 3, 4]

The Roots in Baghdad: Formation of Spiritual Identity in the Milieu of the "Ben Ish Ḥai"

The roots of Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri are planted deep in the spiritual soil of Baghdad Jewry at the end of the 19th century. He was born on the second day of Sukkot, the 16th of Tishrei, the day of the ushpizin of Isaac our patriarch, and was therefore named after him.[2, 3, 4] His father, Rabbi Yeḥezkel Ze'ev Diba, was a merchant of perfumes and spices who supported Torah scholars and engaged in charity in secret, a fact that contributed to the spiritual atmosphere in which his son grew.[2, 4] At that time, Baghdad was a vibrant Torah center under the leadership of Rabbi Yosef Ḥayyim, author of the "Ben Ish Ḥai," whose influence on the young Rabbi Kaduri was decisive.

The encounter between the child Yitzhak and the "Ben Ish Ḥai" is described in many traditions as a defining moment in which a "spark" of blessing and longevity passed. The "Ben Ish Ḥai" blessed the child that he would not need physicians throughout his life, a blessing that indeed was fulfilled as evidenced by his long life history that reached 107 years.[2, 3] The connection to the family of the "Ben Ish Ḥai" continued even after the Rabbi's passing, when members of his family gave Rabbi Kaduri his teacher's personal sash as a gift, an object that symbolized the continuity of the spiritual lineage.[2]

Rabbi Kaduri's early studies took place in "Midrash Beit Zelkha," the elite yeshiva of Baghdad Jewry.[2, 3, 4] Already in his youth he demonstrated extraordinary expertise in Talmud and the halakhic authorities, and at age seventeen he already delivered profound discourses before the Torah greats of the city.[3, 4, 5] However, a central characteristic that would accompany him throughout his life—concealment of his greatness—began already then. His teachers asked him to minimize public discourses out of fear of the evil eye, an instruction that became for him a second nature of modesty and silence.[3, 4, 6] Parallel to his study of the revealed Torah, the Rabbi began to engage secretly in esoteric Torah, drawing from the kabbalistic traditions of the sages of Babylonia, which were characterized by a combination of abstract contemplation with practices of practical Kabbalah.[2]

Milestones in the Baghdad Period and the Beginning of Immigration

The Immigration and Settlement in Jerusalem: The "Porat Yosef" and "Beit El" Yeshivot

In 1922 Rabbi Kaduri immigrated to the Land of Israel, a step that marked the beginning of his second and longest life chapter.[3, 4, 7] He integrated into the leading Sephardic yeshivot of that time, foremost among them Yeshivat "Porat Yosef" in the Old City. In Jerusalem he received great esteem from the local sages, who called him "the lion who ascended from Babylonia" because of the depth of his knowledge.[4, 5] His main teacher at Yeshivat Porat Yosef was Rabbi Efrayim Cohen, with whom he deepened his study of the teachings of the Ari and the Rashash.[7]

The War of Independence and the conquest of the Old City in 1948 constituted a turning point in the Rabbi's life. With the fall of the Jewish Quarter, Rabbi Kaduri moved to study at the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El" in the western part of the city.[3, 4, 5] During this period he continued his modest leadership, while combining intensive study with simple physical labor for his livelihood.

The Ethos of Bookbinding as a Spiritual Act

One of the aspects that distinguished Rabbi Kaduri's figure in these decades was his occupation as a bookbinder.[3, 4, 5] This work was not merely an economic means of avoiding reliance on charity funds, but rather served as a tool for self-learning. By virtue of his role as a bookbinder, rare manuscripts and ancient books in revealed and esoteric Torah came into his hands. The Rabbi would read and memorize the contents of the books before binding them, and thus accumulated vast and unconventional knowledge not found in the common printed books.[3, 4]

This approach of "Torah with labor" enabled him to remain in the shadows for many years. His teacher, Rabbi Amram Aburbia, described him with the expression "his heart is like a lion's heart but appears as a fox," expressing the contrast between his internal spiritual power and his simple and modest external appearance.[6] The ability to conceal his greatness allowed him to develop without external disturbances, until he became the supreme kabbalistic authority of his generation.

His Torah Teachings: The Sanctity of Speech and Hastening the Redemption

The teachings of Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri are not formulated in ordinary contemplative philosophical literature, but rather are embodied in his conduct, his blessings and the conciseness of his words. Two central principles stand at the foundation of his worldview: the sanctity of speech (silence) and the importance of studying Kabbalah as a tool for hastening the redemption.

The Rabbi emphasized ceaselessly the need for guarding one's speech and minimizing idle talk. He viewed speech as a highly powerful spiritual tool that could be wasted or defiled through improper use. His personal conduct of silence and use of short, precise sentences derived from a deep kabbalistic understanding that the sanctity of speech is a necessary condition for the ability "to effect salvations."[1, 2] His regular blessings, such as the verse "and you shall say, 'Thus shall you say to the living one: Peace be to you, and peace be to your house,'" were chosen meticulously as tools for transmitting spiritual abundance while maintaining conciseness.[4, 5]

Additionally, the Rabbi believed that the study of esoteric Torah is not merely a privilege for individuals, but a generational necessity for hastening the redemption. He saw in the afflictions of the people and natural disasters in the world signs of the "birth pangs of Messiah" and urged the public to immigrate to the Land of Israel and prepare for the revelation of the Messiah, who according to him had already begun to act in the world.[2, 8]

The "Naḥalat Yitzḥak" Institution: The Center for Disseminating Esoteric Torah

Toward the end of his life, and with the help of his son Rabbi David Kaduri, the Rabbi established the kabbalists' yeshiva "Naḥalat Yitzḥak" in Jerusalem.[2, 3, 4] This yeshiva became a world center for Kabbalah studies according to the path of the Arizal and the method of the "Rashash" (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi), also called 'Or HaShamash'.[4, 5, 9]

In the yeshiva there exist several study tracks that combine the revealed and esoteric:

Kollelim for Kabbalah: Five kollelim intended for fellows who delve deeply into the writings of the Ari and the intentions of the Rashash.[9]

Kollelim for the plain meaning: Two kollelim engaged in Gemara and halakha studies, out of understanding that the esoteric must rest upon a stable foundation of the revealed.[7, 9]

Community and spiritual activity: Conducting "tikkunim," pidyon nefesh and special prayers for the benefit of the individual and the collective.[9]

The establishment of the yeshiva marked the transformation of the Rabbi from a concealed kabbalist to a public leader influencing thousands of students and those seeking salvation. In this yeshiva prominent students were also trained, among them Rabbi Ya'akov Adas, who assi
in making his writings accessible to the broader public.[4, 5, 10]

The World of Practical Kabbalah: Amulets, Segulot, and Incantations

Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri was renowned as one of the greatest experts in recent generations in the field of practical Kabbalah. This domain, which involves the use of sacred names and mystical formulae to influence reality, was considered dangerous and required extreme caution. The rabbi used to say that he did not engage in conjuring angels, but only in prayer and supplication for divine mercy through those holy names.[6]

The Methodology of Amulet Writing

Rabbi Kaduri's amulets were written according to a meticulous tradition transmitted to him from the sages of Babylonia, particularly from the kabbalist Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya. He was careful not to add or detract from the received formulae, out of reverence for the sacred.[6] His writing was characterized by a "late Oriental" style, a combination of square and cursive script, as can be seen in his diaries and the manuscripts that have been revealed.[11]

The uniqueness of his amulets lay in the principle of "the man was proven and the amulet was proven"—meaning, the power derived both from the sacred text and from the personal sanctity of the writer.[12] There were cases in which the rabbi gave "amulets for swallowing"—notes written in special ink intended to be dissolved in water for healing purposes, an ancient practice permitted by halakhic authorities in cases of danger to life.[12]

Analysis of the Treatment Diaries (1964–1965)

The revelation of the rabbi's personal diaries from the years 1964–1965 provides a rare glimpse into the nature of the appeals to him and his treatment methods. The diaries document over 450 cases of people who sought remedy for their distress.[11]

The use of the term "iz"d" (izeh davar—"something") in the diaries indicates a fixed and secret formula that the rabbi used for common cases, suggesting a systematic and organized method of mystical work.[11]

The Literary Legacy: "Pitḥei Olam" and "Kedushat Yitzḥak"

Although Rabbi Kaduri was known primarily as a man of action, he left behind a written Torah legacy that serves as a foundation for the study of practical Kabbalah and prayer intentions.

The "Pitḥei Olam" Series

This composition, comprising five volumes, is the most comprehensive work the rabbi wrote during his lifetime.[12, 13] The book deals extensively with matters of amulets, segulot, incantations, and prayers. The rabbi consolidates in it all the knowledge he accumulated over decades of work with the public, while explaining the spiritual meaning of each and every action.[12] The book is now considered a foundational text for those engaged in this field within the world of kabbalist yeshivot.

The "Kedushat Yitzḥak" Series

After his passing, a six-volume series entitled "Kedushat Yitzḥak" was published, edited by Rabbi Ya'akov Adas.[7, 10] This series is unique in that it presents photographs of the rabbi's original manuscripts, without alteration, with added commentaries clarifying concepts difficult to read and understand.[10] Among the segulot appearing there:

Revealing one's match in a dream: a special prayer formula for bachelors.[10]

Healing by means of an egg: writing sacred names on a black hen's egg and burying it in ash.[10]

Seeing and invisibility: using psalms combined with intentions for protection from enemies.[10]

Rabbi Adas emphasized that the use of these books requires spiritual preparation and a high level of fear of Heaven, as this involves "holy fire" that can harm one who is unworthy.[10]

Political and Social Influence: Rabbi Kaduri and the Rise of Shas

Rabbi Kaduri's status as "elder of the kabbalists" transformed him into a center of social and political power, especially among Shas movement voters. His blessings and amulets became an integral part of election campaigns in the 1990s.

In the 1996 election campaign, extensive use was made of Rabbi Kaduri's amulets to encourage voting for Shas. This activity provoked a wide-ranging legal controversy, which led to an amendment to the Elections Law (known as the "Amulets Law"), prohibiting the giving of amulets or blessings as part of election propaganda.[14] High Court of Justice rulings at that time attempted to balance freedom of worship and belief against safeguarding the integrity of elections in a democratic state.[15, 16]

Despite the controversy, the rabbi's influence remained immense. Politicians from all parties came to his home to receive his blessing, in recognition of his public power and the quiet charisma he radiated. The meeting with the Lubavitcher Rebbe in 1990 added to his international stature, when the Rebbe prophesied that his name "Kaduri" indicated an influence that would embrace the entire world.[2, 4]

The "Messiah Note" Controversy and Messianic Expectations

In his final years, the rabbi increasingly engaged with matters of redemption. He claimed that the Messiah was already among us and operating "behind the curtain."[8] Shortly before his death in 2006 (29 Tevet 5766), the rabbi left a sealed note in which he wrote that he was revealing the name of the Messiah.[17]

The note, opened a year after his passing, contained the sentence: "Concerning the acronym of Mashiaḥ: he will lift the people and prove that his word and his Torah stand."[17] The initial letters of the words "yarim ha'am veyokhiaḥ" form the name Yehoshua (or Yeshua).[17, 18] This revelation provoked great controversy and conflicting interpretations:

Denials by the family and rabbis: Many in the rabbinic establishment and among his family members claimed that this was a forgery or a distorted interpretation by interested parties.[17, 19] His son, Rabbi David Kaduri, noted that his father always said that the Messiah would be revealed only after the coming of Elijah the Prophet, and such rumors should not be relied upon.[19]

Kabbalistic interpretation: Other rabbis, such as Rabbi Uri Sharki, noted that the name "Yehoshua" is connected to Messiah son of Joseph according to the teachings of the Vilna Gaon and Ramḥal, and there is no allusion whatsoever to Christianity as was claimed on some websites.[18]

The controversy surrounding the note only intensified the myth surrounding the rabbi's figure as a man of mystery whose connection to the supernal worlds continued even after his death.

Summary and Conclusions on the Figure of the "Elder of the Kabbalists"

Rabbi Yitzhak Kaduri was a unique figure in modern Jewish history. He succeeded in combining seemingly contradictory worlds: scholarly genius with simple manual labor; extreme silence with broad political influence; and abstract Kabbalah with practical practices of amulets and segulot.[1, 2, 3, 4]

His principal achievement lies not only in the "miracles" attributed to him, but in the preservation and revival of the tradition of the sages of Babylonia and Jerusalem. His books, "Pitḥei Olam" and "Kedushat Yitzḥak," serve today as the most professional anchor for the study of practical esoteric Torah, while emphasizing the need for sanctity of speech and fear of Heaven as prerequisites for any spiritual action.[10, 12]

Yeshivat "Naḥalat Yitzḥak" continues to serve as a Torah center training the next generation of kabbalists, thereby ensuring that Rabbi Kaduri's legacy will not remain merely a historical memory, but a living and active force in the world of Torah and Kabbalah.[9] His figure remains a symbol of national unity, as hundreds of thousands from all communities and sectors participated in his funeral, united in appreciation for a righteous man who saw himself as merely a simple "bookbinder," yet bore on his shoulders the secrets of the redemption of the Jewish people.[5, 12, 20]
